Schema Inference for Tabular Data Repositories Using Large Language Models

Zhenyu Wu Affiliation: Department of Computer Science
University of Manchester
Manchester, UK
zhenyu.wu@manchester.ac.uk    Jiaoyan Chen Affiliation: Department of Computer Science

Manchester, UK
norman.paton@manchester.ac.uk Affiliation: 
Abstract

Minimally curated tabular data often contain representational inconsistencies across heterogeneous sources, and are accompanied by sparse metadata. Working with such data is intimidating. While prior work has advanced dataset discovery and exploration, schema inference remains difficult when metadata are limited. We present SI-LLM (Schema Inference using Large Language Models), which infers a concise conceptual schema for tabular data using only column headers and cell values. The inferred schema comprises hierarchical entity types, attributes, and inter-type relationships. In extensive evaluation on two datasets from web tables and open data, SI-LLM achieves promising end-to-end results, as well as better or comparable results to state-of-the-art methods at each step. All source code, full prompts, and datasets of SI-LLM are available at https://github.com/PierreWoL/SILLM.

Index Terms: 
Schema Inference, Tabular Data, Large Language Models, Prompt Learning

I Introduction

Tabular data that come from sources such as data lakes contain important data but are often minimally curated, making it hard to analyze [1, 2, 3]. Because such repositories aggregate datasets from diverse producers and publishers, they exhibit schema- and instance-level heterogeneity at scale. As a result, data scientists frequently struggle to identify what relevant data exist and how they can be used in a given analysis.

The difficulty of extracting value from heterogeneous repositories has long been recognized, and many techniques support discovery and exploration [4]. Prior work includes keyword- or example-based dataset search [5, 6], navigation through related datasets [7, 8], ontology-based annotation where suitable ontologies exist [9, 10], and data profiling or join discovery to improve logical schemas [11, 12, 13]. These approaches enrich or navigate metadata, but they do not yield an integrated semantic view of heterogeneous datasets.

Schema inference addresses this gap by seeking to infer a schema that summarizes and organizes a repository’s structure [14, 15, 16], capturing recurring patterns while abstracting representational inconsistencies. For example, tables about the entity type movie may record production companies under different headers (“Production company”, “Studio”) and with varying values (“Warner Bros.” vs. “Warner Bros. Pictures”); schema inference abstracts these into a unified type movie with the attribute production company. Such schemas can be represented in different data models (e.g., relational, E/R, XML Schema, property-graph) to support entity types, attributes, and inter-type relationships [17, 18, 19, 20].

In this paper, we infer a conceptual schema for a repository of tabular datasets. Compared with the underlying logical schemas, which directly reflect table and attribute definitions, the inferred conceptual schema offers a more compact and semantically coherent view of the core concepts represented by tables, together with their attributes and relationships. Inferring such schemas is challenging for two reasons: (i) representational heterogeneity: column headers are often inconsistent or domain-specific, and cell values are variably formatted, which makes it hard to align semantically-equivalent attributes/types of data; (ii) sparse metadata: in data repositories, curated ontologies or training data are rarely available, which constrains the use of external supervision for schema inference.

To address these challenges, we propose SI-LLM (Schema Inference using Large Language Models), a three-step, prompt-based framework that infers a conceptual schema directly from tabular data, using only column names and values, without relying on bespoke training or domain ontologies (Fig. 1(a)).

Our contributions in this paper are as follows:

  1. 1.

    We propose SI-LLM, an end-to-end prompt-based LLM framework that systematically integrates type/hierarchy, attribute, and relationship inference.

  2. 2.

    An evaluation of SI-LLM on two annotated repositories (web tables and open government data), showing consistent improvements over strong baselines: +7–10% Rand Index with ∼\sim97% purity for type/hierarchy inference, performance comparable to or better than PLMs for attribute inference, and +30–40% recall/F1 in relationship discovery.

  3. 3.

    An end-to-end case study with a visualized conceptual schema, illustrating how heterogeneous tables can be integrated into a coherent schema.

II Related Work

Schema inference has been employed for different purposes by a variety of communities. Most research on schema inference has been closely associated with a specific data model and its features. For example, schema inference for XML [21, 22] and JSON [23, 24] tends to infer a schema that can precisely describe a collection of documents, with each document conforming to the inferred schema. This approach is best suited to a collection of largely consistent documents. In contrast, schema inference for RDF [17, 25, 18] tends to assume that the published data may be both diverse and from a variety of typically inconsistent publishers, and thus that the inferred schema is more summarising the contents than inferring a description to which all instances must conform. This ethos is generalised by constructing a graph over different (typically semi-structured) data models in Abstra [26], where the graph is then partitioned into collections that represent recurring structural patterns. NextiaDI [27] also uses a graph model with a focus on the merging of schemas. Approaches for XML and JSON tend to inform the inference process using the names of elements in documents; approaches for RDF may annotate documents with type information, and proposals differ in the extent to which they assume the use of consistent terminology.

Instead of inferring schemas to which the original data must conform, several proposals aim to infer concise summaries that highlight the primary concepts represented in the data sets [19, 16]. Such approaches may take as input a target size for the inferred schema, in which case the objective is then to identify the most representative datasets, which may be those that are extensively connected to others. Although not explicitly on schema inference, ALITE [28] constructs a full disjunction over tables by identifying equivalent columns and producing a unified integration schema. Unlike our approach, which infers a fine-grained, hierarchical schema, ALITE maps all datasets into a single flat table. A related area uses LLMs for domain modelling [29, 30], though building on textual descriptions of domains, rather than collections of tables.

In relation to other work on schema inference, our approach is distinctive in several respects: (i) there is no other approach that focuses on inferring a conceptual schema over heterogeneous tabular datasets; and (ii) we assume that datasets may use highly inconsistent terminologies and representations, and use LLMs to account for such heterogeneity.

III Approach

III-A Problem Definition

Let D={d1,…,dn}D=\{d_{1},\ldots,d_{n}\} be a collection of datasets. Each dataset d∈Dd\in D has columns C⁡(d)={c1,…,cm}C(d)=\{c_{1},\ldots,c_{m}\}; each column cc has a header and cell values V⁡(c)={v1,…,vk}V(c)=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{k}\}. Our goal is to infer a conceptual schema that abstracts and unifies the structural properties across DD. Formally, a conceptual schema is a triple: S=⟨T,H,R⟩S=\langle T,H,R\rangle, where TT is a set of conceptual types. Each t∈Tt\in T has a name t.𝑡𝑦𝑝𝑒𝑁𝑎𝑚𝑒t.\mathit{typeName} and a set of attributes A​t​t​s​(t)={a1,…,ap}Atts(t)=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{p}\}. Each attribute a∈A​t​t​s​(t)a\in Atts(t) is a semantic property of tt that aligns a group of dataset columns a.𝑑𝑎𝑡𝑎𝑠𝑒𝑡𝐶𝑜𝑙𝑢𝑚𝑛𝑠a.\mathit{datasetColumns}, with values drawn from heterogeneous domains (e.g., strings, numbers, dates). Each type tt is also linked to the subset of datasets t.𝑑𝑎𝑡𝑎𝑠𝑒𝑡𝑠⊆Dt.\mathit{datasets}\subseteq D from which it is derived. H=(T,E)H=(T,E) is a directed acyclic graph representing a type hierarchy, where each edge (u,v)∈E(u,v)\in E indicates that uu is a subtype of vv. RR is a set of directed semantic relationships between conceptual types. Each r∈Rr\in R is a triple ⟨ti,ai,tj⟩\langle t_{i},a_{i},t_{j}\rangle, where ti,tj∈Tt_{i},t_{j}\in T and ai∈𝐴𝑡𝑡𝑠⁡(ti)a_{i}\in\mathit{Atts}(t_{i}) is a named entity attribute whose values predominantly refer to instances of type tjt_{j}. Such a triple denotes a semantic link from tit_{i} to tjt_{j} via attribute aia_{i}.

As shown in Figure 1(b), SI-LLM includes three steps:

  1. 1.

    Infer table type hierarchy (S1): given a set of tabular datasets DD, we infer a conceptual type hierarchy for each dataset, with the root type constrained to Thing. These per-dataset hierarchies are then merged into a unified global hierarchy by aligning types that are inferred from individual datasets. Inconsistent edges are pruned via post-merging.

  2. 2.

    Infer conceptual model attributes (S2): Given a direct child type tt of Thing from S1, associated with a cluster of datasets t.datasetst.\textit{datasets}, we label and resolve the columns of these datasets such that each group of aligned columns corresponds to a conceptual model attribute a∈t.attributesa\in t.\textit{attributes}.

  3. 3.

    Discover relationships between types (S3): given a pair of types ti,tj∈Tt_{i},t_{j}\in T, a relationship r⁡(ti,tj)r(t_{i},t_{j}) is established when a named-entity attribute aia_{i} of type tit_{i} semantically refers to instances of type tjt_{j}.

The following subsections provide a detailed explanation of each step.

III-B Type and Hierarchy Inference.

In this step, we construct a global type hierarchy over the table collection DD, where each type t∈Tt\in T is associated with the tables that describe its instances. Rather than predicting the types for each table followed by constructing the is-a relationships via strategies like breadth first search as in [31], we adopt a strategy that directly infers the full type hierarchy of each table from scratch motivated by [32]: for each table di∈Dd_{i}\in D, we extract a conceptual hierarchy Hi=(Ti,Ei)H_{i}=(T_{i},E_{i}), where TiT_{i} denotes the set of types of did_{i}, and EiE_{i} denotes the set of directed edges representing is-a relationships between types in TiT_{i}. To ensure consistency across tables, we root all hierarchies at Thing. We then merge the individual hierarchies by aggregating all parent-child edges and pruning incorrect or inconsistent ones to form the global hierarchy H=(T,E)H=(T,E). The resulting hierarchy organizes tables into groups, where the tables associated with each type define a group. Among these, the broadest groups form the direct children of Thing, which we refer to as top-level types. Their descendants form a layered structure that captures increasingly specific is-a relationships among the inferred types.

Individual Table Type Hierarchy Inference. Here, we describe the method for constructing the type hierarchy for each table. Rather than incrementally inferring is-a relationships between table types, we use the LLMs to infer the complete type hierarchy of each table as a set of top-down paths, with each path capturing the progression from the root type to the most specific type(s).

Figure 3 illustrates the overall type hierarchy inference prompt for an individual table. The input contains records of a table (e.g., about Movie), and the output is a type hierarchy expressed as a type path of length at most NN from the root type Thing to the most specific type that represents the table’s described entities (e.g., Thing → CreativeWork → Movie). In our experiment, we set the maximum path length to N=5N=5, one above the ground-truth hierarchy depth (≤4\leq 4), to allow slack. We use 3-shot prompting, each shot providing: (i) a five-row table sample (as in [33]); and (ii) the ground-truth output path(s) from the schema.org type hierarchy. By default, the model is prompted for a single most-specific path per table; when shots include multiple paths, it may emit multiple lines, which we parse as a set, e.g.: Thing →\rightarrow CreativeWork →\rightarrow SoftwareApplication →\rightarrow VideoGame
Thing →\rightarrow CreativeWork →\rightarrow Game →\rightarrow VideoGame.

When multiple valid type paths exist (e.g., due to multiple inheritance), we list all paths, one per line, even if they diverge mid-path but share the leaf. Unless noted, we report single-path accuracy; multi-path outputs are analyzed separately. For post-processing, we keep the longest well-formed path Thing→t1→⋯→tk\texttt{Thing}\to t_{1}\to\cdots\to t_{k} (each tit_{i} a recognized type), ending at the last valid type; trailing text is ignored. If the path depth exceeds maximum path length, we discard it and re-run the prompt.

Constraints in Prompts. We also explore the introduction of constraints into the prompt design to ensure that inferred individual hierarchies can be effectively merged into a coherent global structure. These constraints are intended to guide the LLMs toward producing more structured and well-formed hierarchies, and we treat them as tunable parameters. Motivated by recent work questioning the stability of ad hoc prompt engineering [34], we have systematically tested whether lightweight, interpretable prompt constraints can boost hierarchy inference. Due to space constraints, in Figure 3 we abbreviate the original instruction as <ORIGINAL INSTRUCTION>. We design four prompt constraints, as shown in Figure 3:

  1. 1.

    Abstract Type Constraint (ABS). We prevent overly generic top-level assignments by blacklisting abstract types. Specifically, we query Wikidata for the first-level subclasses of entity (Q35120) via SPARQL and pass this set to the LLM as an exclusion list.

  2. 2.

    Second-Layer Convergence Constraint (SLC). To promote cross-table coherence, this constraint states that second-layer types (direct children of Thing) should converge across all tables, discouraging divergent top-level types for semantically similar tables.

  3. 3.

    Most specific Type Constraint (FET). We implement this constraint with two standalone prompts: (i) infer the most specific type(s) for a table, and (ii) extend the original instruction (Figure 3) to generate a hierarchy rooted at Thing that terminates at the inferred type(s). Under FET, the inferred type(s) are explicitly inserted into the second prompt rather than passed via conversational context.

  4. 4.

    Full Constraint (FULL). A combined constraint that applies both FET and the SLC constraint.

The evaluation results, presented in Section IV-B2, show that all these prompt constraints enhance type hierarchy inference, but in different ways.

Table Hierarchy Merging and Pruning. The final output hierarchy is obtained by merging and pruning all the individual table type hierarchies. An initial hierarchy is first constructed by directly merging the types and edges from type hierarchies of all the tables. Given the hierarchies H1=(V1,E1),…,Hn=(Vn,En)H_{1}=(V_{1},E_{1}),\ldots,H_{n}=(V_{n},E_{n}), the initial output hierarchy is defined as Hraw=(Vraw,Eraw)H_{\text{raw}}=(V_{\text{raw}},E_{\text{raw}}), where Vraw=⋃i=1nVnV_{\text{raw}}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}V_{n} and Eraw=⋃i=1nEnE_{\text{raw}}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}E_{n}. As a part of merging, we also weight the edges according to the number of times they occur in the collection of individual hierarchies. For each (u,v)∈Eraw(u,v)\in E_{\text{raw}}, we have its weight as w(u,v)=∑i=1n[(u,v)∈Ei]w(u,v)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\!\left[(u,v)\in E_{i}\right], where 𝟏​[⋅]\mathbf{1}[\cdot] denotes the indicator function, which equals 11 if the condition holds and 00 otherwise.
Then the following steps are applied to HrawH_{\text{raw}} for pruning:

  1. 1.

    Self-loop pruning: All edges (u,u)∈Eraw(u,u)\in E_{\text{raw}} are removed.

  2. 2.

    Inverse-edge pruning: Bidirectional edges are turned into unidirectional ones. Namely, for (u,v)∈Eraw(u,v)\in E_{\text{raw}}, if (v,u)∈Eraw(v,u)\in E_{\text{raw}} and w⁡(v,u)>w⁡(u,v)w(v,u)>w(u,v), (u,v)(u,v) is removed.

  3. 3.

    Erroneous is-a relationship pruning: LLMs are known to sometimes generate hallucinations. They occasionally produce inaccurate or noisy is-a relationships when generating individual table type hierarchies. When these hierarchies are merged, such local errors can propagate and compromise the overall structure. For example, the LLM may predict the path Thing → Event → CreativeWork → MusicAlbum, incorrectly placing CreativeWork, which is expected to be a top-level type, under Event. As a result, all subtypes of CreativeWork, such as MusicAlbum, are misclassified under the Event branch, distorting the hierarchy. To address this, we introduce an LLM-based filtering step in pruning. For each candidate parent-child pair, we prompt the LLM with ”Is A the parent type of B? Only answer yes or no.” and remove relations identified as incorrect. Thus we employ peer-LLM verification to cross-check model outputs [35]; this reduces hallucinations in a task-dependent manner but does not provide guarantees, so we also use LLM-as-a-judge as a pragmatic safeguard.

In summary, SI-LLM first generates individual type hierarchies (paths) for each table, and then merges them into one hierarchy, followed by pruning. We hypothesize that, given sufficient table context, the LLM can leverage its pretrained knowledge to infer globally consistent type paths that accurately capture the table semantics. In contrast, the previous approach of first inferring types individually and then constructing their is-a relationships [31] increases the risk of overlooking intermediate types in the hierarchy, which can result in partial or fragmented structures. By generating complete hierarchies (paths) in a single pass, we aim to better exploit the LLM’s capacity for generation and global reasoning with consistency, leading to more accurate and coherent type hierarchies. The empirical comparison of these approaches is presented in Sec. IV-B1.

III-C Attribute Inference

Given the inferred type hierarchy, the second step of SI-LLM is to infer conceptual attributes for each type by abstracting them from columns across the tables assigned to the type. The procedure is presented in Algorithm 1.

For each type tt, we collect columns from tables whose most specific type is tt. Using the prompt in Fig. 4(a), the LLM infers a canonical attribute name for each column from its header and up to k=5k=5 sampled non-null cell values (Lines 1-1). This procedure applies to all columns (numeric, text, categorical, etc.) without customization.

As different columns may yield different inferred attribute names with similar meanings, we run attribute name resolution on all the inferred names (Line 1; prompts shown in Figure 4(b)). Specifically, we provide the names to an LLM and instruct it to group semantically equivalent variants and assign a single canonical representative to each group. For example, the attribute names Producer, Release Company, and Studio, though expressed with slight variations, are expected to be grouped together and resolved to a representative name like Production_Company. When no equivalents exist, we allow a group to contain a single name. The resulting canonical attributes are then assigned to type tt. If tt has child types, we infer inherited attributes for tt by identifying attribute groups that appear in at least a θ\theta fraction of its children and promote them to tt (Line 1-1). In our experiments, we set θ=0.9\theta=0.9. Since inferring inherited attributes requires prior inference of child types’ attributes, we adopt a bottom-up traversal in the general loop (Line 1), starting from the lowest layer and moving upward in the hierarchy.

III-D Relationship Discovery

In this section, we describe how relationships between conceptual types are discovered, potentially in the absence of table-level relationships, by way of the conceptual domains of attribute instances. For example, the type Movie contains the attribute production_company, whose values—such as ”Warner Bros.”, ”Walt Disney Studios”, ”Paramount Pictures Corporation”, ”Sony Pictures Entertainment Inc.”, and ”NBCUniversal, Inc” (see the second column in Figure 3)—are instances of the type Company. This suggests that production_company expresses a relationship between Movie and Company. This observation provides the insight of SI-LLM: when the values of an attribute aia_{i} of type tit_{i} predominantly refer to instances of another type tjt_{j}, aia_{i} indicates a relationship from tit_{i} to tjt_{j}.

Algorithm 2 shows the steps to seek relationships of a given type tit_{i} towards a set of other types TjT_{j}. We first get the attributes of tit_{i} whose associated columns contain named entities. For each such attribute aa, we randomly sample k=5k=5 unique cell values (instances) from its associated table columns (Line 2). We adopt a top-down strategy to narrow candidate types. For each attribute aa, we first predict the top-KK relevant top-level types Ttop′T^{\prime}_{\text{top}} (Line 2), and then select the most specific descendant type tjt_{j} that best matches its instances (Line 2). As shown in Figure 1(a), for the attribute production_company of Movie, SI-LLM selects the top-level type Organization, restricts the candidates to its descendants, and ultimately chooses Company as the most specific type (Figure 4(c)).

Once the target types are determined, the relationship name rr is derived from the semantics of aia_{i} using an LLM (Line 2). The model takes as input the attribute name aia_{i} together with the type pair (ti,tj)(t_{i},t_{j}), and generates a predicate label that captures the relationship expressed by aia_{i}. Continuing the example, the inferred relation is producedBy, linking Movie to Company and reflecting the company’s role in film production.

IV Experiments and Evaluation

IV-A Experimental Setup

IV-A1 Datasets

We use two table sets for evaluation: WDC which includes 602 tables with 237 from T2DV2 [36] and the rest from Web Data Commons [37]), and GDS which includes 660 tables from Google Dataset Search [38]. Each set is annotated with a ground-truth (GT) hierarchy derived from Schema.org, and each table is annotated with both the most specific and top-level entity types. We also manually annotate conceptual attributes based on Schema.org. To construct GT relationships between types, we utilize named entity attributes with reference to Schema.org. If the values of an attribute aia_{i} from type tit_{i} predominantly refer to entities of another type tjt_{j}, we annotate a relationship from tit_{i} to tjt_{j}. The statistics of the datasets are shown in Table I.

IV-A2 Metrics

Metrics for type hierarchy and conceptual attribute inference. Each top-level type (i.e., direct children of Thing) is associated with a group of tables that describe its instances. Since top-level types represent the broadest and typically disjoint categories, we view top-level type inference as an approximate table clustering problem, where each top-level type corresponds to a cluster. Standard clustering metrics are used, including Rand Index (RI): RI=TP+TNTP+FP+FN+TN\text{RI}=\frac{\text{TP}+\text{TN}}{\text{TP}+\text{FP}+\text{FN}+\text{TN}}, where a pair of tables compose a true positive (TP) if they are of the same type and correctly clustered together, a true negative (TN) if they are of different types and correctly separated into two clusters, a false positive (FP) if they are of different types but wrongly clustered together, and a false negative (FN) if they are of the same type but wrongly separated into two clusters. Purity measures the proportion of tables correctly assigned to their GT top-level type, averaged across all the top-level types. Similarly, conceptual attribute inference also adopts metrics of clustering, where Purity is calculated per attribute within each top-level type and averaged over all the attributes.

To evaluate the inferred hierarchy against the GT hierarchy, we propose a Path-based Tree Consistency Score (PTCS). Given a complete path p=[t1,t2,…,tn]p=[t_{1},t_{2},\dots,t_{n}] in the inferred hierarchy HH with t1t_{1} being Thing and tnt_{n} being a leaf type, each type tit_{i} is matched to a type ti′t_{i}^{\prime} in the GT hierarchy H′H^{\prime}. Note ti′t_{i}^{\prime} is regarded as matched if it is the most frequent entity type annotation of the associated tables of tt. This leads to a sequence composed of matched types: p′=[t1′,t2′,…,tn′].p^{\prime}=[t_{1}^{\prime},t_{2}^{\prime},\dots,t_{n}^{\prime}]. A PTCS can be calculated for pp: PTCS(p)=L⁡(p′)|p′|\text{PTCS(p)}=\frac{L(p^{\prime})}{|p^{\prime}|} where |p′||p^{\prime}| is the size of the set of the types in p′p^{\prime}, and L⁡(p′)L(p^{\prime}) is the length of the longest subsequence of p′p^{\prime} that forms a path in the GT hierarchy. In the end, we extract all such complete paths in HH and average their PTCSs as the PTCS of HH. Additionally, we use the count of the number of types, T​#T\#, to measure the diversity of types in HH.

Metrics for Relationship Discovery. We report P​r​e​c​i​s​i​o​n=T​PT​P+F​PPrecision=\frac{TP}{TP+FP}, R​e​c​a​l​l=T​PT​P+F​NRecall=\frac{TP}{TP+FN} and F​1−s​c​o​r​e=2∗P​r​e​c​i​s​i​o​n∗R​e​c​a​l​lP​r​e​c​i​s​i​o​n+R​e​c​a​l​lF1-score=\frac{2*Precision*Recall}{Precision+Recall}, where true positives (TP), false positives (FP), and false negatives (FN) are calculated by comparing the inferred relationships against the set of GT relationships. For simplicity, we sometimes also use P, R and F1 to denote Precision, Recall and F1-score, respectively.

IV-A3 Baselines

Each step in SI-LLM is compared with corresponding baselines. For type hierarchy inference, we adopt GeTT (generative models) and EmTT (embedding models) from [31], where most of the EmTT variants except for EmTT with SBERT use fine-tuned PLMs. For the baselines of attribute inference, we apply hierarchical clustering over embeddings of table columns within each top-level type, with the same PLMs in EmTT adopted for column embedding. For relationship discovery, we adopt a heuristic baseline that identifies relationships from one type tit_{i} to another type tjt_{j}. Specifically, we compare each attribute aia_{i} of tit_{i} against tjt_{j} based on their columns. If the columns of aia_{i} match at least a proportion τ1\tau_{1} of the columns of any attribute aja_{j} in tjt_{j}, we infer a relationship between tit_{i} and tjt_{j}. Note that two columns are regarded as matched, if their embeddings, which are also based on the previous PLMs in EmTT, lead to a cosine similarity larger than τ2\tau_{2}. We set τ1\tau_{1} and τ2\tau_{2} to the values that yield the highest F1 for each PLM.

SI-LLM and the baselines are implemented in Python 3.11 using PyTorch, VLLM and the Hugging Face Transformers library.

IV-A4 Implementation details

We invoke each LLM statelessly and generate with temperature 0.1. To account for randomness, each experiment is run five times and we report the mean. EmTT fine-tuning for Starmie, DeepJoin, and SwAV follows [31]. Qwen2.5-14B runs locally on a single NVIDIA A100 (80 GB) with dual AMD EPYC CPUs and 512 GB RAM.

IV-B Result Analysis

IV-B1 Type Hierarchy Inference (S1)

For top-level type quality, as shown in Table II, SI-LLM consistently achieves the highest Purity scores across all the settings, with almost 99% on WDC and 98% on GDS. Compared to GeTT, which also uses LLMs but follows a chain-of-thought strategy, SI-LLM yields Purity improvements of around 24% on both datasets. It also outperforms most EmTT variants, with Purity gains of up to 17% on WDC and 30% on GDS.

In terms of RI, while SI-LLM does not always achieve the top score, it remains competitive, being close to DeepJoin, SwAV, and most GeTT variants.

This discrepancy between Purity and RI is mainly due to two factors. First, the inferred hierarchies allow semantic overlaps between top-level types (e.g., Product, CreativeWork), whereas the GT adopts mutually exclusive labels. For example, ComicSeries can be considered both a Product and a CreativeWork, depending on the perspective. Such cases increase semantic coherence within clusters (high Purity) but reduce alignment with the GT, which assumes disjoint clusters and thus lowers RI. Second, even for tables representing the same type, individually inferred hierarchies can differ due to variations in reasoning. For instance, a table about art might yield the path Thing → Art → ArtDomainEntity → Painting in one case, while another yields Thing → CreativeWork → Painting, depending on context. When merged, such differences can introduce mismatches at the top-level type, affecting RI.

Beyond top-level types, we also assess the quality of the inferred global hierarchy. As shown in Table II, SI-LLM consistently achieves high PTCS, reaching up to 0.847 on WDC and 0.791 on GDS. Compared to GeTT, SI-LLM shows improvements of up to 15% on WDC and over 30% on GDS, reflecting stronger consistency w.r.t. the GT. In terms of #T, SI-LLM produces hierarchies with rich type coverage (up to 389 types on WDC and 306 on GDS). They are comparable to those of GeTT, and exceed those of EmTT, indicating more fine-grained modeling than embedding-based approaches.

Our PTCS scores are lower than those of EmTT. This mainly stems from the characteristics of LLM-inferred hierarchies, which tend to be more fine-grained and introduce intermediate or abstract types not explicitly present in the GT hierarchy. For example, while the GT hierarchy has a path Thing → Event → SportsEvent → OlympicCompetitions, the inferred hierarchy may generate more detailed paths such as Thing → Sports → Athletics → HighJump → Men’s HighJump or Thing → Sports → Football → FootballPlayer. Although these finer distinctions better capture the semantics of the dataset collection, they reduce structural alignment with the GT, lowering consistency scores. Overall, the results highlight that SI-LLM effectively balances consistency and type richness, achieving robust and generalizable performance across datasets.

IV-B2 Ablation Study

In this part, we study how incorporating different constraints (i.e., the original instruction from Fig.3 denoted as Ori here, and ABS, FET, SLC and FULL as shown in Fig. 3) into the prompt instruction impacts model performance. As shown in Fig. 5 and Fig. 6, we observe that introducing almost any constraint typically leads to improvements across all evaluation metrics. Overall, using FET or FULL as constraints leads to substantial gains in top-level type inference compared to unconstrained prompts (approximately 7% improvement on WDC and 5%-16% on GDS). Meanwhile, employing SLC or ABS as constraints yields more pronounced improvements in the tree consistency of the generated hierarchies (approximately 8%-12% improvement on WDC and 5%-10% on GDS).

IV-B3 Attribute Inference (S2)

The results of conceptual attribute inference are presented in Table III. See below for some key observations.

For the metric RI, SI-LLM consistently achieves strong performance across datasets. Its scores are all above 0.90 on WDC and above 0.95 on GDS, matching or exceeding most embedding-based baselines. On WDC, it outperforms DeepJoin and Starmie by around 12% and 4%, respectively, and is competitive with SBERT and SwAV. On GDS, RI scores are generally high across all methods, partly due to the dataset’s pronounced long-tail distribution, characterized by many small clusters and an imbalanced column distribution, which can inflate RI scores even when Purity is lower.

For Purity, SI-LLM performs well overall, reaching around 0.70–0.74 on WDC and 0.65–0.71 on GDS. On WDC, it consistently surpasses DeepJoin and Starmie, while SBERT, Unicorn, and SwAV occasionally achieve slightly higher scores. On GDS, SwAV produces the highest Purity (0.803), with SI-LLM consistently falling within a 1–10% difference. The lower Purity observed on GDS can be attributed to the larger number of attribute columns, which challenges the LLM’s context capacity and increases the likelihood of grouping errors.

We identify two recurring error patterns in LLM outputs. The first is over-generalization, where loosely related attributes (e.g., game_identifier, game_title, game_description) are grouped under a broad attribute such as Game Info. The second is semantic mixing, where distinct functional attributes (e.g., number_of_user_ratings, number_of_alternates) are merged due to lexical similarity in naming (e.g., both start with “number_of”) rather than their functional role. These issues underscore the limitations of LLM-based grouping when dealing with large, complex attribute sets.

Overall, the results suggest that SI-LLM delivers robust and competitive attribute inference, providing consistent improvements over several strong fine-tuned embedding-based baselines across evaluation metrics.

IV-B4 Relationship Discovery (S3)

We report the relationship discovery (S3) results in Table III. SI-LLM with different LLMs generally achieves higher F1 compared to the embedding-based baselines. On the WDC dataset, SI-LLM (Qwen2.5-14b) shows strong or near-top performance across metrics, while on the GDS dataset, SI-LLM (GPT-4) achieves the highest Recall (0.809) and F1 (0.807). The embedding-based baselines tend to have much lower Recall; for example, SBERT achieves only 0.221 on WDC and 0.097 on GDS.

While the embedding-based baselines can capture instance-level signals, their primary focus is on testing whether table columns are related at the instance level, not whether their concepts are related. As a result, these methods based on column similarity often have difficulty capturing conceptual-level relationships where instance-level similarity does not necessarily imply a meaningful type-level connection. Our LLM-based method helps address this gap by leveraging sampled attribute values together with attribute names to directly infer type-level relationships. This often leads to improvements in Recall and F1. Nevertheless, LLMs may occasionally struggle with differences in the semantic granularity of attribute values. For example, the model may link CreativeWork.Artist to Organization because some artists, such as bands or musical groups, can also be categorized as organizations, while individual artists cannot. This reflects a challenge where attribute values can have different meanings depending on context, which can lead to overly broad or imprecise type predictions.

V Case Study

We apply all three steps of SI-LLM using GPT-4 on the GDS benchmark and present end-to-end results, as shown in Figure 7.

Top-level types. Figure 7(a) shows the inferred top-level types with their attributes and relationships. The schema recovers 87% of annotated types overall; at the top level, 5 out of 6 ground-truth top level types are recovered, including Person, Organization, Place, Event, and CreativeWork, while Product does not appear at the top level. Relationships are inferred from associated attributes—originating either from associated tables (with the current type as their most specific type), or from mutual attributes propagated upward from child types (marked in italic and underlined). All inferred top-level relationships align with the ground truth.

Odd cases. Although Product is missing at the top level, it reappears under the top level type Object. The Object hierarchy (Fig. 7(c)) has Product as its sole direct child, which further refines into subtypes such as Vehicle, Medicine, and Games. While the name of type Object is generic, the internal taxonomy is coherent, as these subtypes can naturally be interpreted as is-a Product. A related issue arises when tables on mobile and video games are grouped under VisualWork, reflecting plausible groupings but imperfect naming.

Person sub-hierarchy. Figure 7(c) illustrates the inferred hierarchy under Person. Attributes such as Name are propagated upward to the parent, since they appear in at least θ=0.9\theta=0.9 of the child types. By contrast, attributes such as Age, Height, and Weight are common in most athlete subtypes but are not promoted. Their absence in a single subtype (e.g., Marathon Runner) keeps them below the θ=0.9\theta=0.9 threshold. Sibling types such as Soccer Player, Basketball Player, and Football Player are supported by distinct table sets, indicating mutual exclusiveness at the table level, consistent with the ground truth.

VI Conclusion and Future Work

Schema inference is a potentially useful technique for helping data scientists and engineers discover and explore relevant data in a repository. To be widely applicable, schema inference should take account of heterogeneous representations and assume minimal metadata. We presented SI-LLM, an end-to-end prompt-based framework that uses LLMs to inform schema inference at a semantic level, covering type hierarchies, attributes, and relationships inferred directly from tabular data. Our evaluation on two annotated datasets showed consistent improvements over PLM-based baselines that rely on column embeddings and similarity. We also analyzed prompt design for hierarchy inference, providing insights into how different constraints affect LLM performance. Finally, we complemented these results with a case study that visualizes a compact inferred schema. SI-LLM achieves these results without labeled data or external ontologies, relying on minimal metadata.

There remain several promising directions for improving schema inference with LLMs. One direction is refining type naming and reducing fallback into overly generic types, aiming for closer alignment with the ground-truth taxonomy. Another direction is enhancing attribute inference to more robustly capture both common and long-tail attributes.
